y-m-83-07.title: A report says rule with fewest possibilities is safest
y-m-83-07.goal: Find report error where count right but conclusion wrong; design rules meeting constraints; judge equal-likelihood assumption behind probability from case count.
y-m-83-07.material: Choose club locker 4-digit code. Each position 0–9. R1 repeats allowed; R2 all four different; R3 repeats allowed but first digit not 0. Student report counts possibilities, but code-selection method not decided.
y-m-83-07.thinking.0: Notice conclusion may be wrong despite correct calculation
y-m-83-07.prereq.0: H3 batch difficulty only, after counting (product rule, permutations) and basic probability; no grade assignment.
y-m-83-07.prereq.2: If possibilities equally likely, probability is 1/(case count)
y-m-83-07.s.s1.prompt: Report compares 4-digit locker rules by possibilities. Choose line with faulty reasoning. [4 1]
y-m-83-07.s.s1.hint.0: For each rule, say how many choices when you choose and try one code.
y-m-83-07.s.s1.hint.1: Compare guess chance with 5040 vs 10000 possibilities.
y-m-83-07.s.s1.line.0: R1 repeats: each of 4 slots has 10 options, 10⁴=10000. [0 9 10 10 10 10 10000]
y-m-83-07.s.s1.line.2: R3 first not zero, repeat allowed: 9×10×10×10=9000. [0 9 10 9 10 10 10 9000]
y-m-83-07.s.s1.line.3: Possibility count R2<R3<R1. Fewest R2 safest.
y-m-83-07.s.s1.line.4: Therefore no-repeat rule makes code safer.
y-m-83-07.s.s1.explain: Counts 10000,5040,9000 correct. But fewest possibilities isn't safest: guesser has harder time as possible values increase. Line5 repeats same mistake. [1 3 10000 5040 9000 4 5]
y-m-83-07.s.s2.prompt: Design own rule: ≥1,000,000 codes; easy remember, length ≤5. Character-set k from 10 digits, 26 lowercase, 36 digits+lowercase, 62 digits+letters both cases; repetition allowed. Find 3 (k,n).
y-m-83-07.s.s2.hint.0: Choose k,n and calculate codes; check if n=5 insufficient for some k.
y-m-83-07.s.s2.hint.1: Set n=4,5 and compare minimum k needed. [4 5]
y-m-83-07.s.s3.prompt: Want say 'under R1, one-try chance guess code is 1/10000'. Which assumption needed?
y-m-83-07.s.s3.hint.0: In real life, are all 10,000 codes chosen equally often? [10000]
y-m-83-07.s.s3.hint.1: Where does 'equally likely' enter probability calculation 1/10000?
y-m-83-07.s.s3.o.a: Code must be memorable, like 1234, and no repeats.
y-m-83-07.s.s3.r.a: Memorable codes are tried first, making them easier to guess.
y-m-83-07.s.s3.o.b: Guesser must already have tried once or twice unsuccessfully.
y-m-83-07.s.s3.r.b: Previous attempts aren't first-try probability. What event does 1/10000 describe?
y-m-83-07.s.s3.o.c: The 10,000 codes chosen equally likely, and guesser knows rule. [10000]
y-m-83-07.s.s3.r.c: You see reciprocal-of-cases probability needs equal-likelihood assumption.
y-m-83-07.s.s3.o.d: Rule must be changed to R2 no repeats.
y-m-83-07.s.s3.r.d: This doesn't concern R1 rule. Changing to R2 changes case count itself. [] R1.
y-m-83-07.s.s3.explain: For reciprocal case-count to be probability, codes need equal chance. If people choose birthdays or 1234 often, actual chance higher. Possibility count only one security factor.

y-m-83-01.title: Can expression fitting five points say week 10?
y-m-83-01.topic: Function models fitting data and out-of-range predictions
y-m-83-01.goal: Follow finding quadratic fit, revise predictions/confidence with new measurements, state trustworthy range.
y-m-83-01.material: Science club grows kidney bean indoors. Measure stem same weekday/time with ruler, round nearest cm; same water/light each week. Data revealed stepwise; at each step decide week-5 height.
y-m-83-01.thinking.0: Choose model from how growth changes
y-m-83-01.thinking.2: Use reality limits to state model range
y-m-83-01.prereq.0: Task is inquiry after linear/quadratic functions. H3 is batch difficulty label, no grade assignment.
y-m-83-01.prereq.1: Find and compare weekly increases from table
y-m-83-01.s.s1.prompt: As weekly bean height data arrives, choose view of week 5 (later week 10); revise as data grows. Keeping first view okay with evidence.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.hint.0: When new data arrives, first compare your prediction with it.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.hint.1: Put weekly increases side by side and inspect how increase changes.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.0.info: Indoor kidney bean; same day/time, ruler to nearest cm, same water/light. Measurements: week1 4cm, week2 7cm, week3 12cm.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.0.ask: Need predict week5. With only current data, most reasonable way to state?
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.0.after: Three points fit different models. Increase changing from 3 to 5 questions assumption 'same growth each week'.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.0.o.a: Increase went 3cm,5cm, so give a range depending on assumptions, don't lock one value.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You consider limited evidence and changing increases, separate predictions by assumption.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.0.o.b: From 4cm week1 to 12cm week3 growth 8cm, assume 4cm each week and predict 20cm at week5.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You summarize with average growth, but actual increase changed 3 to 5. Did you test 'same every week'?
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.0.o.c: Increase itself rose by 2 (3 to 5); assume +7 week4, +9 week5, predict 28cm, and measure more to check.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You turn change in increase into assumed rule, but note three points require checking.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.0.o.d: Only three measurements, so better give no week-5 number.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.0.r.d: Caution is good, but stating assumption and range differs from saying nothing.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.1.after: If increases keep rising 3,5,7,5th week height matches n²+3 for weeks1–4, predicting 28cm at week5. But fitting four points isn't proof it continues. [2 3 5 7 3 1 4 28 5]
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.1.o.a: I keep 20cm prediction from data through week3, don't change it. [20 5 3]
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.1.r.a: Week4 already 19; 20 at week5 means just 1cm growth. Does that fit previous 3,5,7? [4 19 5 20 1 3 5 7]
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Average hides increase pattern 3,5,7. Inspect trend before averaging. [3 5 7]
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Increase rose 2 each week: 3,5,7, so week5 around 19+9=28cm. [2 3 5 7 5 19 9 28]
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You extend increase-change rule to predict.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Rule seems plausible, but only four points; predict around 28 and check week5.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.1.r.d: Week5 measured 28cm matching prediction; week6 36cm. n²+3 gives 39 at n=6. Variety description: stem stops around 60cm.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.2.info: Can report week10 prediction from expression (103cm)? Decide using all data/description. [5 28 6 36 6 3 39 60]
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.2.ask: Even if fit five points, week6 differs and reality caps at 60cm. Extrapolation is weak, but no reason to discard expression entirely. [10 103]
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.2.after: Week6 36cm must be measurement error; ignore and report expression's week10 value 103cm. [5 60]
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Calling any mismatch error makes formula unfalsifiable. Is 3cm due to error or growth slowing? [36 6 103 10]
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Use formula only within week1–6 data; say week10 hard to trust due to 60cm limit and week6 gap. [3]
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.2.o.b: You distinguish model's fit range from outside. [1 6 10 60 6]
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Expression misses week6, so discard quadratic and restart linear.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.2.o.c: One miss makes you discard model fitting 5 points. How far was it right and where did it fail? [6]
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.2.r.c: Don't decide from week6 alone. Measure weeks7,8 too; state week10 only as formula value. [5]
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.2.o.d: You delay judgment but specify needed info. [6 7 8 10]
y-m-83-01.s.s1.st.2.r.d: At first one value uncertain; with more data formed assumed rule. In final, separate fit range from extrapolation? Explain what changed or evidence backing unchanged view.
y-m-83-01.s.s1.reflect: What else needed to make week10 prediction more reliable? Choose all.
y-m-83-01.s.s2.prompt: For each option say how info changes what you say about week10.
y-m-83-01.s.s2.hint.0: When expression and week6 disagree, which info helps explain why? [10]
y-m-83-01.s.s2.hint.1: Weekly heights of other plants under same conditions [6]
y-m-83-01.s.s2.o.a: Check whether one plant pattern repeats across plants.
y-m-83-01.s.s2.r.a: Write stem height more precisely to 2 decimal places
y-m-83-01.s.s2.o.b: More precision doesn't answer whether formula continues. Is missing precision or range?
y-m-83-01.s.s2.r.b: Whether pot light, temperature, water changed after week6
y-m-83-01.s.s2.o.c: Check whether conditions for model changed. [6]
y-m-83-01.s.s2.o.d: Calculation 103 already right. Arithmetic correctness differs from real-world validity. [103 10]
y-m-83-01.s.s2.r.d: Information on maximum height of this variety [103]
y-m-83-01.s.s2.o.e: Compare model value with real limit.
y-m-83-01.s.s2.r.e: More precise writing or calculation only refines calculation. To know if model continues, need outside-model info: other plants, condition changes, real limits.
y-m-83-01.s.s2.explain: Even other-plant data and max height reduce uncertainty a lot; condition-change record better.
y-m-83-01.s.s2.acc.0: Knowing conditions and max height helps set model range. One plant's random variation remains.
y-m-83-01.s.s2.acc.1: How report week5 and week10 predictions in 1–2 sentences? Include numbers and trust level (range/conditions).
y-m-83-01.s.s3.prompt: First distinguish which of weeks5 and 10 lies within measured range.
y-m-83-01.s.s3.hint.0: For each, give data-based reason value could be wrong. [5 10]
y-m-83-01.s.s3.hint.1: Example: For weeks1–6 data ... but week10 ...
y-m-83-01.s.s3.placeholder: You give different trust levels for week5 vs week10? [1 6 10]
y-m-83-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Writing separates fit range and extrapolated range? [5 10]
y-m-83-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: You cite week6 36 vs predicted39 or 60cm cap?
y-m-83-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Weeks1–6 fit n²+3 well and week5 was 28cm. But week6 measured 36 vs model 39 and variety limit ~60cm, so week10 model value 103 is far beyond measurements and not trustworthy.
y-m-83-01.s.s3.model.0: I expect week10 around 60cm or less. Formula gives103 but checked only through week6, so outside values are reference only. [1 6 3 5 28 6 36 39 60 103 10]
y-m-83-01.s.s3.model.1: You state usable range without discarding model. [10 60 103 6]
y-m-83-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: Week5 about 28cm (error 1–2); for week10 only say ≤60cm; use n²+3 only weeks1–5.

y-m-83-02.title: Estimating value with simulation and error [100 3.12 3.14]
y-m-83-02.topic: Find overconfident claims in report estimating π by random points; state repeated-result scatter limits; design more reliable experiment.
y-m-83-02.goal: Estimate π with simulation. Computer randomly uniformly places points in square 0≤x≤1,0≤y≤1. If x²+y²<1, point lies inside quarter-circle radius1. Quarter-circle area π/4, square area1, so probability inside is π/4. One group uses 100 points and writes report.
y-m-83-02.thinking.2: Task inquiry after probability (area, repeated trials). H3 batch level only, no grade.
y-m-83-02.prereq.0: Circle area formula and quarter-circle meaning [] H3.
y-m-83-02.prereq.1: Probability as area ratio (no SD formula needed)
y-m-83-02.prereq.2: This is report from one group. Choose line where evidence insufficient. (Line numbers shown from 1 on screen.)
y-m-83-02.s.s1.prompt: Classify each line as observed, calculated, or concluded. [1]
y-m-83-02.s.s1.hint.0: If repeat once, will exactly 78 appear?
y-m-83-02.s.s1.line.0: Among them, 78 meet x²+y²<1 (inside quarter circle). [100]
y-m-83-02.s.s1.line.1: Probability inside is area ratio π/4, so say 78/100≈π/4. [1 78]
y-m-83-02.s.s1.line.4: With 1000 points, result will certainly be closer to 3.14. [3.12 3.14]
y-m-83-02.s.s1.line.5: Line 5 treats 3.12 from 100 points as exact π; line 6 says more points 'certainly' closer. Random repeat gives different result; more points usually reduce spread, no guarantee one estimate closer. Lines1–4 ratio→π/4→×4 are usable. [1000 3.14]
y-m-83-02.s.s1.explain: Five groups each place 100 points: inside counts 78,81,74,80,77. Estimates: 3.12,3.24,2.96,3.20,3.08; mean 3.12. How judge 'experiment shows π<3.14'? [5 3.12 100 6 1 4 4 4]
y-m-83-02.s.s2.hint.0: Compare that range with gap between 3.14 and 3.12.
y-m-83-02.s.s2.hint.1: 3.12 closest to 3.14, so that group did most accurate experiment.
y-m-83-02.s.s2.o.a: This confuses one result close by chance with method accuracy. Inspect repeated-result scatter. [3.12 3.14]
y-m-83-02.s.s2.o.b: Averaging reduces scatter, but 500 points still may not resolve 0.02 gap. Assess trust in average. [3.12 3.12 3.14]
y-m-83-02.s.s2.r.b: Results range 2.96 to 3.24, so with 100 points can't say anything about 3.12 versus 3.14. [500 0.02 3.12 3.14]
y-m-83-02.s.s2.o.c: You compare repeated scatter (0.28) against target difference (0.02), seeing scatter far larger. [2.96 3.24 100 3.12 3.14]
y-m-83-02.s.s2.r.c: Each group differs, so experiment tells nothing about π. [0.28 0.02]
y-m-83-02.s.s2.o.d: Different results don't mean useless. Knowing scatter width lets us still say π about 3.
y-m-83-02.s.s2.r.d: Five results range 2.96–3.24 (scatter ~0.28); desired difference 0.02 is much smaller. Can't tell 3.12 vs 3.14; can only say π around 3.
y-m-83-02.s.s2.explain: Design same quarter-circle experiment more reliably. Specify point count and repeats, and in 2–3 sentences what conclusion it can support. [2.96 3.24 0.28 0.02 3.12 3.14 3]
y-m-83-02.s.s3.prompt: First say what repeating same experiment (five groups) teaches. [2 3]
y-m-83-02.s.s3.hint.0: Compare effect of increasing point count versus repeat count.
y-m-83-02.s.s3.hint.1: Example: Repeat placing ... points ... times, and ...
y-m-83-02.s.s3.placeholder: Why include changing point number and repetitions?
y-m-83-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: What say when results cannot distinguish 3.12 and 3.14?
y-m-83-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Instead of 'accurate', state limit such as 'within this range'? [3.12 3.14]
y-m-83-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Each group repeats with 1000 points 5 times. Inspect range of five estimates; if both 3.12 and 3.14 fall inside, don't claim which closer.
y-m-83-02.s.s3.model.0: Place 400 points each time, repeat 10 times for 10 estimates. Fourfold points should halve spread, roughly. If results still differ, treat as error; don't declare π<3.14. [1000 5 5 3.12 3.14]
y-m-83-02.s.s3.model.1: I state expected link between point count and scatter. [400 10 10 4 3.14]

y-m-83-04.title: Comparing by splitting into groups (interpreting data)
y-m-83-04.topic: When overall and device-specific ratios differ, check equal comparison conditions; revise judgment/confidence and explain with numbers.
y-m-83-04.goal: School library app alternates recommendation phrases A/B and records clicks. App, not students, decides which access device (mobile/PC) sees which phrase. Data arrives stepwise; judge which phrase gets more clicks.
y-m-83-04.material: A school library app alternates recommendation phrases A and B and records clicks. The app, not students, assigns which device (mobile or PC) sees each phrase. Data arrives in stages; each time judge which phrase gets more clicks.
y-m-83-04.prereq.0: Assumption about school order: dem see dis as inquiry task after learning ratios and conditional ratios for probability and statistics. 'H3' na only label for difficulty level of production batch, e no assign grade.
y-m-83-04.prereq.1: Finding and comparing ratios with fractions and percentages
y-m-83-04.prereq.2: Understanding how sample size affect how much you fit trust a ratio
y-m-83-04.s.s1.prompt: Data to find out which recommendation phrase for school library app, A or B, get more clicks dey come out stage by stage. For each stage, choose your judgment and think whether new information change your judgment or confidence. You fit keep your judgment too if you get evidence.

y-m-83-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You follow direction of device results and also talk about uncertainty where sample small.

y-m-83-04.s.s1.st.1.r.d: You reduce information because e complicated. See wetin disappear when you reduce am.
y-m-83-04.s.s1.st.2.info: When dem check how dem show phrases, A show 100 of its 120 times to PC users, and B show 100 of its 120 times to mobile users. If you combine both phrases, mobile click ratio na about 56% (67 out of 120) and PC about 19% (23 out of 120).
y-m-83-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: Now wey you know dis information, wetin judgment make sense?

y-m-83-05.title: We fit say monthly compounding na 6% yearly because '0.5 times 12'?
y-m-83-05.topic: Comparing Interest Models and Judging Information We Need
y-m-83-05.goal: Use numbers test claim wey compare monthly compound interest with yearly simple interest, sort information we need to state conclusion, and find and explain by yourself how difference change with period.
y-m-83-05.material: One student see bank advert and talk, 'Compound deposit wey add 0.5% interest every month na 0.5×12=6, so e same as deposit at 6% simple interest per year.' For compound interest, each month interest join principal to calculate next month's interest; for simple interest, dem calculate interest only on original principal. For this task, assume no tax or charges.

y-m-83-06.title: If five examples work, proof don finish?
y-m-83-06.topic: Explaining Number Properties with Reasons Instead of Examples
y-m-83-06.goal: Judge difference between adding examples and explaining every case, find rule by making numbers wey fit a condition, and explain reason with place value to person wey no trust examples.
y-m-83-06.material: Minsu say e find rule after calculating few values of three-digit number minus number wey dem write backwards. 752−257=495, 841−148=693, 931−139=792, 620−026=594, 504−405=99. All these values be multiples of 99 (99×5, 99×7, 99×8, 99×6, 99×1). For this task, subtract reversed number from bigger number (drop leading 0, so 026 count as 26).
y-m-83-06.prereq.0: Assumption about school order: dem see am as inquiry task after learning polynomial operations and factoring. 'H3' na only label for production batch difficulty, no be grade assignment.

y-m-83-06.s.s1.prompt: Minsu calculate few values for three-digit number minus reversed number (752−257=495, 841−148=693, 931−139=792, 620−026=594, 504−405=99). All be multiples of 99. Minsu talk, 'Five examples work, so value from this kind subtraction always be multiple of 99, and proof don finish.' (Subtract smaller number from bigger. 026 count as 26.) Wetin you think about this statement?
y-m-83-06.s.s1.hint.0: Roughly think how many three-digit numbers Minsu never check.
y-m-83-06.s.s1.hint.1: Think wetin happen to claim if even one example no work.
y-m-83-06.s.s1.o.a: Even with plenty examples, some numbers never checked, so dem need reason wey work for every number.
y-m-83-06.s.s1.r.a: Dem notice say for 'all numbers,' wetin dem need na reason, no be number of examples.
y-m-83-06.s.s1.o.b: E correct five times, so we fit talk say na enough proof.
y-m-83-06.s.s1.r.b: Dem treat plenty correct examples like e mean every case work. Think whether one more example still fit fail.
y-m-83-06.s.s1.o.c: Na only five examples, so we suppose think claim likely wrong.
y-m-83-06.s.s1.r.c: Dem conclude claim likely false because examples few. Few examples and wrong answer na separate things.
y-m-83-06.s.s1.o.d: If we check every three-digit number wey we fit check, without missing any, e become proof.
y-m-83-06.s.s1.r.d: When possible cases finite, checking all of dem without exception na proof too. But if cases plenty, e no efficient.
y-m-83-06.s.s1.explain: Few examples working no be proof. To prove am, you must show 'reason wey work for every case' or check all possible cases without missing any.
y-m-83-06.s.s1.acc.0: Three-digit possibilities finite (~400 cases subtract smaller from larger); exhaustive check is proof, but general explanation more efficient.
